name: Adam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager at Lindenhof Dairy, a family business that milks five hundred cows and grows maize, grass and some wheat on about three hundred and fifty hectares. The Brandt family own it, and I run the cows with a team of six. I'm in at five, look at the overnight data from the collars on the cows, check the fresh calvers, and then it's breeding, feeding plans and staff rotas, with a quick AI check on the ration most mornings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy getting the numbers to move: more milk per cow, fewer lame cows, a better calving interval. I use AI tools every day for the rations and the breeding lists, and I'd not go back. What wears me out is the money. The pay's modest for the job, and for three years we've been helping pay my father's care home, so with two kids and a mortgage there's next to nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, nothing more, and that's fine by me. I'd say farmers who use it well will do a bit better than those who don't. That's how it's always been with any new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I keep doing well at a job that doesn't pay quite enough. I'd keep finding small gains. The care home bill doesn't care about AI either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep pushing the Brandts to tie part of my pay to the herd's results. I'd try a couple more AI tools for heat detection. And I'd look at a small side job, maybe advising another dairy one day a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient, because I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your father's care.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He had a stroke four years ago and he needs full-time care now. My sister and I split the top-up fees. It's what you do for your parents, but it's emptied our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever resent that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. He worked forty years on farms to give us a start. I'd just like a bit of slack so a broken car doesn't feel like an emergency.

S0.say: It's a decent tool, nothing more, and that's fine. Farmers who use it well will do a bit better than those who don't, like with any new kit.
S0.think: I keep doing well at a job that doesn't pay quite enough. I'd keep finding small gains, and the care home bill doesn't care about AI either way.
S0.do: Keeps running the herd and asks the owners to tie part of his pay to herd results. Tries more AI tools for heat detection and looks at advising another dairy one day a month for extra income.
S0.feel: Calm, a little impatient because he likes a challenge.
S0.quote: It's what you do for your parents, but it's emptied our savings.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is numbers-driven and already uses AI daily without fuss. His thin savings come from paying for his father's care, which he sees as a plain duty. He's looking for small gains and side income even in the quiet picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for farmers who are ready, and a wake-up call for those who aren't. I'd say the answer is to learn, not to complain. I'd say that at the discussion group and on the dairy forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do well out of this. The Brandts would need someone who can run robot milkers, feed pushers and collars, and I already know the systems. My worry is for the lads on the team who don't want to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd push the Brandts to put in robot milkers on half the herd and manage the switch myself. I'd do the manufacturer's training, which is a couple of weeks. And I'd offer weekend help to smaller dairies setting up the same kit, for cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kevin. He's been milking for twenty years, he's quick and he's careful, but he won't touch a tablet. I'd try to get him onto the hoof care, because robots don't do that well yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for anything from the Brandts in return?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pay rise, plainly. If I save them three milkers' wages, I'd want a share of that. If they said no, I'd know my worth on the market.

S1.say: This is good news for farmers who are ready and a wake-up call for those who aren't. The answer is to learn, not to complain.
S1.think: I'd do well out of this, because the owners would need someone who can run robot milkers, feed pushers and collars, and I already know the systems. My worry is for team members who don't want to learn.
S1.do: Pushes the owners to put robot milkers on half the herd in the first year and manages the changeover himself after the manufacturer's training. Offers weekend paid help to smaller dairies setting up the same kit.
S1.quote: If I save them three milkers' wages, I'd want a share of that.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an opportunity and is clear he would benefit. He thinks in terms of his market value and would ask for a share of savings. His concern for a long-serving milker was specific and practical, moving him onto hoof care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people should get moving rather than wait for the government to save them. I'd say families and communities need to pull together. I wouldn't be calling for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's harder than I'd say in public. If the robots can manage the herd as well as I can, the Brandts don't need a herd manager, just someone to call the dealer. I'd have maybe a year of being useful while they set it up, then I'm out with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the most of that year. I'd learn everything about the new systems and offer myself as an installer to other dairies, through the dealer or on my own. We'd cut back at home straight away, and I'd talk to my sister about whether we can keep up the care home fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, but my stomach would be in a knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jakob and Mia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That Dad's job is changing and we're going to be careful with money for a while. Jakob's twelve, he'd ask if we're moving. I'd tell him not yet, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people should get moving rather than wait. Is that fair to people who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Kevin can't move like I can. Maybe that's where family and the community come in, because the government's too slow anyway.

S2.say: It's a shock, but people should get moving rather than wait for the government to save them. Families and communities need to pull together, not ask for handouts.
S2.think: It's harder than I'd say in public. If robots can manage the herd as well as I can, the owners won't need a herd manager, so I'd have maybe a year of being useful and then be out with nothing saved.
S2.do: Spends the first year learning every part of the new systems and offers himself as an installer to other dairies, through a dealer or independently. Cuts household spending straight away and talks with his sister about keeping up their father's care fees.
S2.feel: Anxious and busy, with his stomach in a knot.
S2.quote: If the robots can manage the herd as well as I can, the Brandts don't need a herd manager, just someone to call the dealer.
S2.fieldNote: His public message is self-reliance, but privately he sees his own job going within about a year. When asked whether that's fair to slower workers, he conceded the point honestly. The care home fees are what make thin savings so pressing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone willing to work at it. I'd tell young farmers to get trained on the robots and the data, and I'd say apprenticeships matter more than degrees now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Five years is enough to make myself the person dairies call when they put the robots in. I'd be forty-eight, still with the mortgage and Dad's fees, but I'd have a trade that's in demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the manufacturer's certification and start doing setups for small dairies at weekends. By year two or three, I'd want to go out on my own as a dairy robot consultant, with a van and a laptop. I'd save the side money to have three months' cushion before I left the Brandts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Like before a big calving week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm grabbing whatever comes. With five, I can build a proper business and leave the Brandts on good terms, maybe even with them as my first client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jakob about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn a skill with his hands and his head, like an electrician or an engineer. Something that still needs a person to turn up. And to never assume a job's safe just because it's always been there.

S3.say: Five years is enough for anyone willing to work at it. Young farmers should get trained on robots and data, and apprenticeships matter more than degrees now.
S3.think: I think I'd be all right, with five years to become the person dairies call when they put robots in. I'd be 48 with the mortgage and Dad's fees, but I'd have a trade in demand.
S3.do: Gets the manufacturer's certification in the first year and does weekend robot setups for small dairies. Saves the side money toward a three-month cushion and aims to go independent as a dairy robot consultant by year two or three.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, like before a big calving week.
S3.quote: With two, I'm grabbing whatever comes. With five, I can build a proper business and leave the Brandts on good terms, maybe even with them as my first client.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets his adaptability turn into a business plan. He'd still want a cushion before leaving his job, which shows caution under the confidence. His advice to his son centres on work that needs a person to turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and anyone who's still surprised in 2036 wasn't paying attention. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let people adapt. Help with apprenticeships, fine, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'm calm about this one. Ten years is time to build up a business, clear some debt and get the kids through school. Dad might not be with us by then, God keep him, and the fees would stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the certifications this year and build the side business slowly. In five years I'd want my own van, a few regular dairy clients, and a bit of savings. I might invest in a second-hand robot milker to rent out to small farms that can't afford a new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if by 2036 the robots set themselves up too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd find the next thing. Maybe training people, maybe running a small herd of my own, maybe something I haven't thought of. I've always landed on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd land on your feet. What if you didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lean on my family and they'd lean on me, the way we have with Dad. That's what family's for. I'd not want the state doing it.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time, and anyone still surprised in 2036 wasn't paying attention. The government should help with apprenticeships but otherwise keep out of the way.
S4.think: I'm calm about this one. Ten years is time to build a business, clear some debt and get the kids through school, and Dad's care fees might have ended by then.
S4.do: Starts certifications this year and builds the side business slowly toward his own van and regular dairy clients within five years. Considers buying a second-hand robot milker to rent to small farms.
S4.feel: Calm, as if he can see the road ahead.
S4.quote: Then I'd lean on my family and they'd lean on me, the way we have with Dad. That's what family's for.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he is at ease and treats AGI as a business opportunity. His fallback is family, not the state, consistent with his traditional views. He spoke of his father's death with a mix of grief and plain realism.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose my job before I'd built anything to replace it. What would help is training paid for by the industry, and apprenticeships so people can learn the new kit fast. Not handouts, just a ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about caring for parents. A lot of people my age are paying for a mum or dad in a home. That's why there's nothing in the bank, not because we're careless.

headlineQuote: A lot of people my age are paying for a mum or dad in a home. That's why there's nothing in the bank, not because we're careless.
portrait: Adam Wagner is a 43-year-old herd manager at a large family-owned dairy who uses AI every day and loves pushing the herd's numbers, but has almost no savings because he helps pay for his father's care home. He believes in self-reliance and family over government help. He's calm in the hype and steady pictures, expecting to gain from running robot milkers. A two-year AGI arrival makes him anxious because he'd lose his job before building anything new, while five or ten years let him plan to become an independent dairy robot consultant, with family as his fallback.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he'd lose his job before he had time to build anything to replace it.
whatWouldHelp: Industry-paid training and apprenticeships so people can learn the new equipment quickly; a ladder, not handouts.
